title: Delhi Air Turns Severe as Outdoor Workers Bear Brunt of Smog
excerpt: The capital recorded an AQI of 403 on Friday morning, and the workers who cannot stay indoors — traffic police, vendors, sweepers and delivery staff — face the longest exposure.
body:
• Delhi's air quality turned severe on Friday, November 13, with an average AQI of 403 at 7 a.m., according to the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) — the first severe reading of the season.
  • Of 58 monitoring stations reporting at 8 a.m., 33 were in the severe category; IIT Delhi recorded the highest AQI at 488, followed by Chandni Chowk at 479.
  • Outdoor workers — traffic police, construction workers, street vendors, road sweepers and delivery workers — have little choice but to stay exposed for long hours, unlike people who can work from home.
  • If you must go out in Delhi: wear a properly fitted N95 mask outdoors, avoid early-morning walks, and check the CPCB's daily AQI bulletin before planning outdoor activity.

Delhi woke up on Friday, November 13, to its first severe air day of the season. According to the Central Pollution Control Board, the city's average Air Quality Index stood at 403 at 7 a.m., crossing into the severe band of 401 to 500. The CPCB classifies AQI between 201 and 300 as poor, 301 and 400 as very poor, and 401 and 500 as severe. Two days earlier, the CPCB's daily AQI bulletin had already recorded Delhi at 313, in the very poor category, with PM2.5 and PM10 as the prominent pollutants.

The Hindu reported that outdoor workers in the capital are reporting breathing difficulties, cough and burning eyes as the air worsens. That picture matches the Union Health Ministry's National Centre for Disease Control (NCDC) health advisory on air pollution, cited by ET Edge Insights, which identifies coughing, breathing difficulty, wheezing, chest discomfort, irritation of the eyes, nose and throat, headaches and giddiness among the possible effects of short-term exposure.

The workers who cannot stay indoors

Health advisories recommend reducing outdoor physical exertion when air quality deteriorates, and at very poor and severe levels people are advised to avoid outdoor activities while vulnerable groups remain indoors. For many Delhi workers, that advice is not an option. As ET Edge Insights notes, traffic police personnel, construction workers, street vendors, road sweepers and delivery workers may have little choice but to remain exposed for extended periods, and cannot avoid the air they breathe during working hours.

The NCDC advisory warns that prolonged exposure at poor AQI levels can cause breathing discomfort even among otherwise healthy people, and that at very poor levels prolonged exposure can lead to respiratory illness in healthy individuals. Exposure can also aggravate asthma, bronchitis and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and long-term exposure can contribute to chronic respiratory and cardiovascular illnesses.

What doctors are seeing

Hospitals are already reporting the strain. Dr Avi Kumar, Additional Director and Head of the Department of Pulmonary Medicine at Fortis Escorts, told The Daily Jagran that Fortis hospitals in Delhi had recorded a 7 to 10 per cent increase in outpatient cases and a 5 to 7 per cent rise in admissions over the previous three to four days, with more cases of allergies, pneumonia and respiratory infections, including among people who had never had breathing problems before. Dr Tanu Kumar, a paediatrician at a Delhi government hospital, reported nearly a 5 per cent increase in respiratory cases in her outpatient department, with more asthma, chest infections, prolonged coughs and a greater need for nebulisation.

“For the general population, to sum up: in winters, try to avoid early morning walks. If you at all have to go, then go with an N95 mask.”

— Dr Girish Sindhwani, Head of Pulmonary Medicine, AIIMS Rishikesh

Dr Kumar said an N95 mask with a proper seal can filter up to 95 per cent of particulate matter. Doctors also advised staying hydrated, limiting physical activity outdoors, and seeking immediate medical attention for a drop in oxygen levels, unusual breathlessness or a fever that does not subside.

How the air got this bad

The deterioration began well before Diwali. According to the Centre for Science and Environment's analysis of official monitoring data, cited by ET Edge Insights, Delhi's average PM2.5 concentration in the week before Diwali stood at 236 micrograms per cubic metre — the highest for that period in three years, 97 per cent higher than the 120 micrograms recorded in 2025. On November 6, the Commission for Air Quality Management invoked Stage III measures under the Graded Response Action Plan across Delhi-NCR as unfavourable weather restricted the dispersion of pollutants. For diaspora families with parents and relatives in Delhi, the practical steps are the ones doctors repeat: check the CPCB bulletin each morning, keep outdoor exertion to a minimum while AQI stays above 400, and make sure anyone who must work outside has a properly fitted N95.
